Development guide

Product implementation

Turn an agreed change into working software with evidence that it meets the intended behaviour. Use this page to plan the work, check the results and prepare for release and learning from use.

Product owners, designers, architects, engineers and reviewers can use this playbook with agreed scope, relevant constraints and supporting evidence. A bounded maintenance change may begin from its issue and existing requirements. If you manage product work, start with the six activities to see what you contribute and what evidence to ask for. Engineering and assurance readers can continue into the optional technical references.

Read the implementation playbook, follow the worked example or consult the optional reference toolkit. Use the EDS AI Workflow for the Eitri delivery procedure.

How the implementation loop works

Implementation repeats as the team builds a change, checks its behaviour and learns from use. Return to Project Discovery when findings challenge the user need or intended outcome. For how these activities connect in the AI-Software Development Lifecycle (AI-SDLC), read the lifecycle overview.

The product requirements document (PRD) describes the intended behaviour and constraints. User interface (UI) artefacts show the experience where relevant. The technical requirements document (TRD) records the engineering approach. Use existing records where they provide this information; the diagram shows how it flows through the work.

Use the six numbered activities to organise the change, scaling the records to its scope and risk. Existing requirements and designs can support a small fix without a new Project Discovery exercise. Verification failures return to implementation; delivery improvements return to planning, while questions about intended value or behaviour return to Project Discovery.

Improve two things at once

The loop improves two systems:

  • The product: its usefulness, usability, reliability, safety, performance, cost and fit with users’ work.
  • The delivery system: the context, tasks, agent instructions, tools, tests, reviews, release controls, monitoring and recovery used to produce the product. This guide calls that system a software factory.

The same failure often needs both responses. A local fix restores the current increment; a change to the delivery process aims to prevent recurrence and is checked on later increments. Read about software factories.

Decide what must be checked before work moves on

Before a task starts, its owner records the required behaviour, expected result and reviewer. Before accepting the change, an independent reviewer compares the actual result with those criteria. A failed criterion returns the change for correction and retesting; an unclear criterion returns to Product, Design and Engineering for a decision.

Keep the requirement, technical decision, task, test result and acceptance decision linked. This connection is traceability: a reviewer can follow a requirement through the work and see which evidence supports it. Record the build checked, unresolved findings, decision maker and next permitted action. Acceptance of a change and permission to release it remain separate decisions.

See how a failed retry check changes the decision in the worked example.

Playbook · Prepare the inputs

Start from the PRD and UI artefacts

See the corresponding decision in Maya’s example

Use Project Discovery’s handoff checklist to locate the agreed scope and supporting records, within the lifecycle handoff agreement. The recommended checks below help the delivery team decide whether it has enough information to plan the change. Project Discovery supplies new product evidence; an existing service can also supply current requirements, designs and operating records. Confirm applicable constraints with their architecture, policy and domain owners.

Recommended implementation-readiness checks
InputInformation to useEvidence it is ready
PRDProblem, target users, scope, user stories, acceptance criteria, non-functional requirements, dependencies and exclusionsAn accountable owner is named, assumptions are visible and acceptance criteria are testable
UI artefactsRepresentative screens or prototypes with interaction rules, states, responsive behaviour, accessibility and intentional deviations; HTML screens and a design.md file are one working formatCritical journeys can be walked end to end, including loading, empty, error, permission and responsive states
Validation and technical evidenceResearch and experiment results, feasibility spikes, approach options, data and integration checks, confirmed dependencies, cost ranges and owned unknownsThe delivery team can explain the evidence limits, the feasible first scope and which remaining checks could reopen Project Discovery
Product measurement planProject Discovery’s success measures, linked to the product North Star where established, with definitions, baselines, targets, guardrails, data sources, collection work, owners and review decisionsThe team can plan instrumentation and data checks, explain how results will be reviewed after use, and identify any baseline gaps with owners and resolution dates
Organisational contextArchitecture, business, domain, policy, security, data, operational and technical constraintsContext is current, authoritative, scoped, attributable and available to each agent that needs it

For services without a user interface, use application programming interface (API) or event contracts and representative interactions instead of screens. Apply the package to the scope being changed; it does not require every product decision to be settled before implementation starts.

Let the PRD define intent, not design

The PRD sets the problem boundary, desired outcomes, observable behaviour and constraints, and leaves legitimate implementation choices to the TRD. A PRD that dictates internal design suppresses engineering judgement. A PRD without acceptance criteria forces implementers to invent product policy. Both create hidden risk.

Note

Using AI to develop software does not mean the product contains AI. If AI output affects the product’s behaviour, that output may vary for the same request: this is probabilistic behaviour. Product and domain owners define which mistakes are unacceptable, who could be affected, permitted data use, when a person takes over and how success will be checked. Engineering and reviewers test those rules on agreed cases, including failures. Use the optional evaluation guidance to plan those checks.

Use UI artefacts to make behaviour concrete

Screens and prototypes show layout, navigation, content density and important states. Record interaction rules, responsive behaviour, accessibility semantics and design decisions alongside them. A design.md file can hold these details when the team uses HTML screens. When the experience changes, update the artefacts, acceptance criteria and related tests together.

Treat organisational context as part of the specification

Architecture standards, domain rules, policies, security controls, operating constraints and business priorities define what a valid implementation is. Without them, an agent can produce work that is correct locally but incompatible with the wider system.

Before planning, Product, Design and Engineering should review the scope, validation evidence and technical findings together with delivery contributors.

Trace a critical journey from the requirement to its design and supporting evidence. Record missing criteria, conflicting constraints and the person responsible for resolving each gap before dependent work begins. Return unknowns that could invalidate the core concept to Project Discovery, or narrow the scope. Carry other accepted unknowns as bounded assumptions, each with an owner, next check, review date and trigger to reconsider the investment.

Next step: walk one critical UI or interface journey, including error and permission states. Link each state to an acceptance criterion and record any missing behaviour with an owner.

Playbook · Translate intent into tasks

Translate intent into executable work

See the corresponding decision in Maya’s example

Specification-driven development makes expected behaviour and design decisions explicit before implementation. GitHub Spec Kit describes a specification, planning and task workflow; this guide uses PRD and TRD as its local document names. The PRD defines required outcomes, the TRD records how the system will deliver them, and tasks turn those commitments into small units that can be verified. Read about spec-driven development.

From product intent to executable work
LayerQuestion it answersMain contentsQuality test
PRDWhat outcome and behaviour are required?Problem, users, scope, stories, acceptance criteria, non-functional requirements, dependencies, exclusionsDoes the team agree what success means?
TRDHow will the system deliver that behaviour?Architecture, interfaces, data, identity, security, operations, rollout, monitoring, trade-offsAre key decisions explicit, feasible and reviewable?
TasksWhich small changes will create and verify it?Feature slices, implementation subtasks, dependencies, tests, evidence, review routes, completion criteriaCan each task be completed and verified without reinventing intent?

Use the TRD as a decision record

A strong TRD explains the affected components, integration boundaries, data flows, API or event contracts, storage, identity and authorisation, failure handling, monitoring, performance, migration, rollout, rollback and unresolved risks. Each major decision traces to the PRD requirement it serves. Recording non-goals, alternatives considered and rejected trade-offs stops later tasks from silently redesigning the system.

Write tasks as units of verification

A task is ready when it describes a bounded change and a reviewer can compare the result with explicit expected behaviour. It links to the PRD acceptance criteria and TRD decisions it implements. It also names its change boundary, dependencies and execution environment, the checks its risk requires, the evidence expected and its independent review route. The EDS AI Workflow turns this into eight issue-verification criteria and a human readiness gate.

Give each agent enough context, and no more

Relevant context helps an agent work within the intended scope, but does not guarantee correct output. Manage context like a product: versioned, attributable, scoped to a domain or repository, discoverable and checked for freshness. Give an agent enough to make the current decision, and disclose deeper guidance only when the task, risk or uncertainty justifies it. Log the context and tools used, so reviewers can reconstruct what informed an outcome. See which context the EDS AI Workflow loads at each stage, or read about context engineering.

Playbook · Build and deliver

Plan, build, check and learn

See the corresponding decision in Maya’s example

Use these six activities to organise a change. Here, “you” means the product manager, product owner or business analyst contributing to delivery. Agree the actual allocation with your team. The named acceptance authority decides whether the change meets its criteria; the release authority separately decides whether it may go live.

In Learn, compare what happened with the PRD’s outcomes and the TRD’s assumptions, and separate product causes from factory causes. If the evidence shows the product intent was wrong, not just its delivery, return it to the Project Discovery loop.

Plan rollout and recovery before release

Release and observe limits how many people a faulty change can affect. A canary release exposes a change to a limited portion of traffic first; Google’s SRE Workbook explains how comparing it with the existing version can reveal failures that pre-release tests miss. It limits exposure; it does not guarantee a safe release.

Before release, record the initial audience, observation period, stop thresholds and who can halt the rollout, and rehearse recovery. Check whether recovery must also restore data or reverse external actions: rolling back code may not undo a migration, a sent message or an automated decision. For an AI capability, record the model, prompt and retrieval configuration with the release.

AIHow AI can help

Give an agent one agreed task, its acceptance criteria and permitted tools. It can propose code and tests, run checks and correct findings within scope. Independent reviewers inspect both code and tests and reproduce important results; retain the diff, check results and exit decision with the increment.

Next step: for the change your team is working on now, identify its current activity and record the evidence and authorised decision needed next.

Playbook · Verify independently

Govern progress with gates and independent checks

See the corresponding decision in Maya’s example

An exit gate is not a meeting or a status label. It evaluates named evidence against named criteria and records who made the decision. Automated gates suit deterministic rules, such as tests passing, schema compatibility, dependency policy and vulnerability severity. People are needed for judgement, trade-offs, risk acceptance and product interpretation.

A strong gate records the evidence it evaluated, the policy version, blocking and advisory findings, exceptions, the approver, the time and the next permitted action. That record lets the team give agents more autonomy without losing the ability to audit what happened.

Separate correction from assurance

Use automated tests and scanners to give the implementer fast feedback. Then have reviewers or independent automated checks examine the change against the agreed acceptance criteria. Keep the acceptance decision separate from producing the change.

Use a human decision where the applicable procedure requires approval, interpretation or risk acceptance. Automation can authorise a routine action only within explicitly delegated scope, criteria and permissions. If that authority is absent or the criteria are inconclusive, refer the decision to the authorised person. The diagram below shows the route with human acceptance.

Move judgement earlier; review by exception

For a consequential or unfamiliar change, compare credible options and agree the important constraints before implementation starts. A short design session or pairing can surface trade-offs while the team can still change direction. Keep that work proportionate to risk and uncertainty.

Automate checks that have deterministic answers, such as formatting, known security findings and agreed architecture rules. A fitness function is an automated check for an important design constraint. Keep agent-generated changes small enough to verify against one agreed outcome, rather than passing a large batch to a reviewer.

Human review is most useful by exception: for a fundamental architecture change, a sensitive security boundary, a large blast radius, an unfamiliar critical system or a change the team cannot confidently explain. This does not remove applicable gates, independent checks or the authorised acceptance decision. It moves the judgement that helps the team make a better change to an earlier point in the work.

In the asset-management example, the team can agree annual-verification permissions and duplicate-task constraints before an agent implements the schedule. They then review the data model, start endpoint, worker and screen as separate verifiable changes. A human reviewer gives extra attention to the permission and inspection-authority boundaries; automated checks cover repeatable rules.

The lanes distinguish who produces the work, who reviews it independently and who decides. Sensors and scanners can include compilers, type checks, static analysis, security checks, contract tests and accessibility checks. Their results support the decision; an exception request does not itself authorise release.

Separation of duties
RoleCanShould not do alone
Implementation agentCreate changes, run tests and scanners, fix findings and assemble evidenceAccept its own work or suppress independent blocking findings
Specialist review agentReview within a defined remit, reproduce evidence, raise findings and confirm fixesApprove outside its remit or accept business risk
Review coordinator (person or automation)Route reviews, merge duplicate findings, track closure and compile the quality reportTurn unresolved disagreement into a silent pass
Accountable personWeigh trade-offs and accept work within delegated authority; refer exceptions and risk acceptance outside that remit to the applicable authorityApprove an exception solely because they are accountable for the change

Make verification independent in practice

A second agent can repeat the first agent’s assumptions. Independence depends on evidence and permissions, not the number of agents: reviewers check acceptance criteria against the original user need, reproduce results and inspect changes to tests as well as code, and release permissions stay outside the implementer’s control.

Record the acceptance check

The reviewer uses the versioned requirements, change set and test results to compare actual behaviour with the agreed criteria. Reproduce checks whose failure would materially affect users, inspect changed tests for weakened expectations, and record the build, conditions, findings and evidence links. Return failed criteria for correction and repeat the affected checks. Refer missing criteria to Product, Design and Engineering; record an unresolved result until the expected behaviour is agreed.

Build testing into implementation

Unit tests give fast feedback on local behaviour, integration tests check contracts with dependencies, and end-to-end tests protect critical user journeys. Choose the mix by the change’s risk and architecture; no single layer is enough.

  • Define expected behaviour and checks before implementing the change. Test-driven development is one way to work from an executable failing test.
  • Before changing an existing service, use characterisation tests to record how it currently behaves. Check that the captured behaviour is still intended; an existing defect is not automatically an acceptance rule.
  • Mutation testing deliberately changes code to introduce faults and checks whether the tests detect them. Use it where worthwhile to find weak assertions; line coverage only shows which code ran during tests.
  • Treat flaky tests as defects with an owner, and make test data, dependencies, models, prompts and environments reproducible.

What the documented Eitri checks require

These are configurable harness defaults; confirm the applicable revision and repository configuration before relying on them.

  1. Readiness: human gates sign off the TRD and approve verified issues before execution.
  2. Build and tests: formatting, type checks or compilation, tests and the production build pass; coverage is at least 80%.
  3. Quality and compliance: any Critical or High finding blocks progress.
  4. Mutation testing: optional and recommended; when used, the default minimum score is 70% on changed files.
  5. Closeout and release readiness: collect the applicable review, architecture, browser and end-to-end evidence; pre-production reruns readiness gates for the Tech Lead’s release sign-off. Closeout alone does not permit rollout.

Check the maintained readiness gates, build thresholds, closeout step statuses and pipeline and release-readiness requirements.

Check AI-assisted work against the same requirements

When an agent develops software, check its actual changes and tool actions against the task and permissions. A convincing explanation is not evidence that the saved records or user journey are correct. Independent review still checks the result.

When the product itself contains AI, test its variable responses and failure behaviour against the product rules as well. The optional evaluation reference explains repeated trials and how to combine automated checks with human assessment.

A useful quality report brings together the linked PRD acceptance criteria, test and evaluation results, scanner and policy findings, open exceptions or remaining risk, and the acceptance decision and authority for the defined scope. For material architecture, security or release decisions, reviewers use the independent judgement check to distinguish the agent’s conclusion from the evidence. Record any separate release approval required by the applicable procedure.

Next step: look at the last change your team merged. Identify who, other than its author, decided it was acceptable, and where that decision is recorded.

Worked example · One continuous delivery story

From an agreed pilot to working software

Follow the fictional asset-management story from Project Discovery. Maya is a project manager who uses the application; the product team decides what to build with her input. Maya’s team agreed to pilot member reporting, annual declarations and manager follow-up for one project. The delivery team must turn this into working software, verify it, release safely and learn from use. The people, results and technical choices are illustrative.

The story connects PRD → TRD → tasks → implementation → independent verification → controlled release → learning. The annual-verification feature runs through the decisions.

Can the team start implementation?

Worked exampleReadinessSee how the team checks requirements, constraints and unresolved questions.

Before development planning, Product, Design and Engineering compare the prototype with the PRD. They walk through:

  • Alex handing the monitor to Priya;
  • Alex reporting the faulty laptop;
  • Alex completing an annual declaration.

For each task, confirm that the acceptance criteria describe the expected result, including failure and recovery. Maya confirms the annual schedule and who will act on reports.

Chapter 3 of 7 · PRD → TRD → tasks

How does the team turn intent into tasks?

Worked exampleRequirements, design and tasksSee how product requirements connect to technical decisions and small development tasks.

Follow one feature through the PRD, TRD and development backlog. The PRD explains the user’s need and expected behaviour. The TRD chooses the technical approach. Tasks divide that design into changes a developer can implement and a reviewer can verify.

PRD: define the scope and user story

The asset-management PRD describes the application’s purpose and users. Its scope covers:

  • importing assets and recording assignments and acknowledged handovers;
  • letting members report lost or faulty equipment;
  • running annual verification and collecting member declarations;
  • giving Maya a dashboard for overdue responses and follow-up;
  • defining access, accessibility and data-retention requirements.

Keep exclusions and unresolved assumptions alongside that scope. For this feature, annual verification means collecting member declarations and reviewing exceptions. A physical inspection remains a separate activity with its own evidence.

User story: As a project manager, I want to start annual asset verification for my project so that members can confirm the assets they hold and I can follow up missing or faulty equipment.

Acceptance criteria for the annual-verification story:

  • Authorised start: Maya can start verification for her project and selected year, with an agreed asset scope and due date. A member or another project’s manager cannot start it or change its records;
  • Annual schedule: the configured yearly schedule starts the same process automatically. A manual start or repeated request for that project and year reuses the existing run;
  • Member tasks: each asset in scope has one current declaration task. Retrying processing preserves existing tasks, saved responses and reminder history;
  • Notifications: members are notified when their tasks are ready and receive a link and due date. Pending or failed notifications remain visible for follow-up; accepting a start request does not imply that messages have been delivered;
  • Accurate responses: members can confirm an asset is present and working or report a fault, loss, an asset not with them or a pending handover. The application saves each response against the correct asset;
  • Manager review: Maya can see completed and overdue declarations and reports needing action. Missing replies remain overdue, and a declaration never automatically marks an asset as physically inspected.

These criteria describe observable product behaviour. They leave the programming language and message-processing design to the TRD.

TRD: explain the choices that protect the requirement

Engineering chooses background processing so Maya can leave the start screen while member tasks and notifications are prepared. Manual and scheduled starts use the same rules. The design must keep one annual run per project and year, one current task per asset, and every saved response when processing repeats.

The team separates “tasks created”, “notifications sent” and “members replied” in the status view. Maya can then follow up the right problem. Engineering records how access checks, stored records, retries and recovery preserve those distinctions.

Tasks: make each choice checkable

  1. Store runs, tasks and responses: test that repeated requests cannot create duplicate work or replace a saved declaration.
  2. Start and process the annual run: test manual and scheduled starts, denied access and interrupted processing.
  3. Notify members and show progress: test failed sends and distinguish notification status from member responses.
  4. Collect responses and support Maya’s follow-up: test permissions, overdue work, keyboard access and the complete dashboard journey.

Link each task to its acceptance criterion, technical decision and expected result. Build shared records and interfaces before dependent workers and screens; independently verify the complete journey after the individual tasks.

Optional engineering detail: Java, React and AWS design, retries and full task breakdown.

Chapter 4 of 7 · Implement

Can the team build and test the workflow?

Worked exampleImplementSee how the team builds a workflow and tests its behaviour.

Implement and test the workflow

The developer first tests the spreadsheet import against known assignments. Flag duplicate asset IDs and send ambiguous assignments for reconciliation. Preserve valid existing records rather than guessing who holds an item.

Build Alex’s reporting workflow and connect it to the annual tasks and Maya’s dashboard. For the retry requirement, use test-driven development: write a failing automated test, then implement the change until it passes. The developer’s first test repeats a start request after a declaration is saved, using a simulated task store. It checks that service’s response, but does not exercise message redelivery against the real database or the dashboard query. Passing it is evidence for one part of the change.

Use a controlled test clock to exercise:

  • the annual check’s opening date;
  • reminder dates;
  • the point when an unanswered task becomes overdue.

Test a member leaving and an acknowledged handover while the annual check is open. Preserve declaration history and route outstanding work according to the reviewed rules. Attach the code diff and test results to the change, with any unresolved findings.

Read the general principle behind this decision

Chapter 5 of 7 · Verify

Does the change meet acceptance criteria?

Worked exampleVerifySee how independent tests expose a defect and confirm its correction.

Verify the implementation against acceptance criteria

Acceptance criterion: retrying the same annual run leaves one current task per asset and preserves any saved declaration. The independent reviewer tests the release candidate, meaning the build proposed for release. Earlier prototype results do not establish whether this build meets the criterion.

The independent check uses the real test database and dashboard, covering the integration omitted from the developer’s simulated-store test. The reviewer saves Alex’s declaration that the laptop is faulty, interrupts the scheduled job and retries it. The application creates a second task. Maya’s dashboard reads the new unanswered task and hides the saved fault report. The job completes successfully, but the application fails its acceptance criterion.

Raise a reproducible defect report. Include:

  • the build ID and test configuration;
  • the steps and test data used to reproduce the failure;
  • the expected and actual results;
  • task IDs, the saved declaration and supporting logs;
  • the result shown on Maya’s dashboard.

The developer fixes task creation and the dashboard query. Confirmation testing repeats the failing scenario to check the fix. Regression testing then exercises related permissions, handovers and follow-up workflows to detect unintended changes.

Worked quality report: the same requirement, two candidates

Illustrative report for the annual-verification change. Roles, decision times, build labels and results below are fictional. In a real report, identify the actual people and link the immutable build, configuration, policy revision and original test records. Coverage and mutation scores do not override a failed acceptance criterion.

Annual-verification quality report
CandidateEvidence and findingsDecision and next action
A · before correctionEvidence and findingsBuild A, test configuration A. Automated checks pass; coverage 86%; optional mutation score 74%. Independent retry evidence: two tasks for one asset, saved fault report missing from the dashboard. One blocking acceptance failure.Decision and next actionIndependent engineering reviewer records the failure. Delegated acceptance owner returns A for correction on 7 November 2026 at 10:00. Retain the before-fix retry run and defect report. Release status: blocked.
B · after correctionEvidence and findingsBuild B, test configuration B. Automated checks pass; coverage 88%; optional mutation score 75%. Independent retry evidence: one task, original declaration retained and visible. Confirmation and related permission, handover and follow-up regression checks pass; no unresolved blockers or exceptions.Decision and next actionIndependent engineering reviewer records the passing retest. Delegated acceptance owner accepts B on 7 November 2026 at 11:00, retaining the after-fix retry and regression reports. Release status: awaiting the separate rollout, monitoring and recovery assessment.

The report links each finding to the acceptance criterion, test run and build. A pending or missing required check leaves the decision unresolved. Compare the documented default checks; use the applicable procedure for the real release.

Keep the decision evidence. Attach the defect report and both test runs to the quality report. The authorised person decides whether to accept the change; the release owner separately reviews release readiness. Verifying this software behaviour does not confirm that the laptop was physically inspected.

Chapter 6 of 7 · Release

Can the pilot be released and recovered safely?

Worked exampleReleaseSee how rollout, monitoring and recovery protect the pilot.

Release the pilot and monitor it

After release approval, use a staged rollout by enabling the application for one project. Before enabling it, confirm:

  • the opening register has been reconciled;
  • Maya’s follow-up queue has an owner;
  • the declaration and reminder schedule is agreed.

Set monitoring thresholds and stop criteria using the product measurement plan and operational requirements.

Rehearse the recovery runbook: the instructions for containing a fault and restoring service. Interrupt the annual job after task creation, retry it, and compare:

  • task IDs and task counts;
  • saved declarations;
  • the audit trail;
  • Maya’s dashboard.

If a report disappears, pause affected task creation and reminders. Preserve member responses and keep the review queue available where safe. Roll back the faulty code or configuration to the last known-good version.

A rollback cannot recall sent reminders or correct data already changed. Reconcile affected records and obtain the applicable authorisation for data corrections. Record who decides when processing can resume. Investigate any unauthorised cross-project update or false inspection record before expanding the rollout.

Read the general principle behind this decision

Chapter 7 of 7 · Learn

What should the team improve next?

Worked exampleLearnSee how observed outcomes guide the next change.

Review outcomes and prioritise the next change

At the agreed review date, Product, Design, Engineering and Maya compare the pilot with the baseline. Review:

  • accuracy of asset assignments and condition records;
  • lost or faulty items awaiting action;
  • overdue declarations;
  • follow-up time;
  • Maya’s effort managing the queue.

Use these results to assess whether the pilot improves accountability. Submission counts alone do not establish that outcome.

Triage duplicate annual tasks as a software defect and add a reproducible case to the development backlog. If members cannot identify their equipment, return to problem research in Project Discovery. If the reports are accurate but Maya cannot act, review ownership and capacity before adding features.

Record the next action and its owner, with the evidence needed to assess the result. Review delivery performance alongside product outcomes and cost. See a worked delivery-measure comparison for this pilot. A fast release does not establish a benefit from AI assistance, and an accelerated scheduling test cannot demonstrate a full year of reliable operation.

Read the general principle behind this decision

After the pilot: fix implementation issues within delivery, or reopen Project Discovery when outcomes challenge the value or intended solution.

Optional applications of this guidance to the asset-management case.

Worked exampleFunctional requirements and acceptance criteria

The PRD defines what the pilot project will support:

  • assigning assets to members;
  • transferring an asset after the recipient acknowledges it;
  • reporting lost or faulty equipment;
  • completing annual declarations;
  • reviewing reports and recording follow-up.

For each requirement, write acceptance criteria that describe the expected result and the conditions in which it applies.

Worked exampleThe implementation agent’s responsibilities

The implementation agent develops the annual workflow and runs its automated tests in the test environment. It submits the code changes and evidence showing whether the acceptance criteria pass. Production data changes and release approval remain outside its permissions.

Worked exampleIndependent test review

The specialist reviewer compares the change with the PRD and test cases. The reviewer:

  • reproduces the retry scenario;
  • tests interruption and restart;
  • inspects database records and the audit trail;
  • checks that assertions verify saved responses rather than discarding them.

Record failed criteria and return them to the implementer for correction.

Worked exampleReview findings and the quality report

The review coordinator consolidates duplicate findings and keeps disputed conclusions visible. The quality report links each finding to its requirement, test evidence and resolution status. Open blocking findings remain visible to the person deciding whether to accept the change.

Worked exampleChange acceptance and exception handling

The authorised person reviews the defined change and its quality report, then records acceptance or requests rework. They refer access exceptions or changes to inspection authority to the relevant owner. Acceptance of the change does not replace the separate release decision.

Worked exampleTesting and quality-gate evidence

Choose tests that exercise the requirement at different levels.

  • Unit tests: check declaration state transitions and due-date calculations;
  • Integration tests: check permissions, concurrent handovers and retries across the API, database and scheduled job;
  • End-to-end tests: complete member reporting and manager follow-up through the UI, including keyboard navigation.

Use characterisation tests to capture valid behaviour before changing the existing import. For the retry defect, keep the failing scenario as a regression test after the fix.

Use mutation testing to assess whether tests detect meaningful faults. Introduce deliberate changes that:

  • remove the unique-task constraint;
  • ignore a conflicting transfer version;
  • mark every declaration as physically inspected.

The relevant tests should fail. If they pass, strengthen the assertions. Assign an owner to flaky tests and fix the source of instability rather than rerunning until they pass.

Keep the quality-gate decision traceable. Record:

  • the build ID and configuration versions;
  • applicable acceptance criteria and policy versions;
  • test and code-analysis results, with blocking findings clearly identified;
  • exceptions and their resolution or approval status;
  • the decision maker, decision time and next permitted action.

A hidden fault report fails the relevant acceptance criterion and blocks that change until corrected. An exception request is referred to its authorised owner; requesting it does not approve a release.

Evaluate a development agent against the task and its permissions. Repeat the annual-job fix on representative cases and inspect:

  • the final database state;
  • changes to test assertions;
  • attempts to use tools outside its permissions.

Evaluate an optional product assistant separately. Use a held-out test set, kept separate from development and tuning, that includes:

  • unclear asset identifiers;
  • sensitive member details;
  • misleading instructions embedded in a report;
  • urgent fault descriptions.

Repeat trials with recorded model and tool versions. Automated checks assess whether the assistant submits to the correct asset and preserves the member’s facts. They also check confirmation and duplicate prevention. People assess clarity and handover to a person. Compare model-based scoring with those human judgements, and retain corrected failures as regression cases.

  • Observability: log task IDs and outcomes so the reviewer can compare database records with Maya’s dashboard;
  • Contract testing: verify expected interactions with identity, scheduling and notification services when those integrations change.

Worked example · Engineering detailJava, React and AWS implementationInspect service choices, retry controls and the full task sequence.

This technical supplement expands the fictional annual-verification design. Return to the main story’s design decisions.

TRD: design the Java and React implementation on AWS

For this fictional implementation, Engineering keeps Java/Spring Boot and React and selects managed AWS services for hosting and background processing:

  • React with TypeScript on Amazon S3 and CloudFront: serve the frontend build from a private S3 bucket through CloudFront. The screens call the Java API for application data;
  • Java with Spring Boot on Amazon ECS with AWS Fargate: run the API and background workers as separate container services, so their deployment and scaling can be managed independently;
  • Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL: store verification runs, declaration tasks and responses, with notification attempts and the audit trail. Use database transactions and uniqueness constraints to preserve consistency;
  • Amazon Simple Queue Service (SQS): use standard queues for background work. Separate scheduled start commands from task-generation jobs and notification jobs, with dead-letter queues for repeatedly failing messages;
  • Amazon EventBridge Scheduler: trigger annual starts and reminder checks on the configured dates and time zones. It dispatches work; the Java services apply the business rules;
  • Amazon Simple Email Service (SES): send verification links and reminders. Record send attempts separately from delivery feedback and member responses;
  • Amazon CloudWatch: collect logs and metrics and raise alarms for worker failures, growing queue backlogs and messages arriving in dead-letter queues.

Use AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) task roles to limit each service’s AWS permissions, and AWS Secrets Manager for database credentials. The Java API still enforces project and member permissions using the application’s organisational sign-in.

This design reuses Java for the API and workers while AWS manages the queue service and database infrastructure. The TRD records the deployment settings and trade-offs, including regional availability and operating cost. The service choices illustrate the asset-management example.

Request and processing flow: manual and scheduled starts reach the same Java start service. SQS separates request handling from background work, so React can show progress while the workers continue processing.

  1. Accept a manual or scheduled start. React submits Maya’s request to the Java API, which checks permissions and returns a run ID and status. For an automatic start, EventBridge Scheduler sends a command to a dedicated SQS queue. Its Java worker invokes the same start service under a restricted service identity. Both routes create or reuse the run for that project and year;
  2. Persist the work to be queued. Save the new run and its pending event in one database transaction. This is the transactional outbox pattern: an event waits in the database until a relay sends it to the task-generation SQS queue. Mark it as published after SQS confirms the send;
  3. Create member tasks. A Java worker on Fargate receives the task-generation message from SQS and creates one task per asset. A database uniqueness constraint on the run and asset prevents duplicates. For each member, save the tasks and pending notification event in one transaction, so a notification job cannot be lost between those writes. The outbox relay then sends that event to the notification SQS queue;
  4. Send notifications asynchronously. A separate Java worker receives notification jobs from SQS and calls SES to email each member the task link and due date. It records the attempt and the SES message ID. Notification processing does not block Maya’s start request;
  5. Collect and display responses. React reads run status from the API and shows task-generation progress separately from notification status. Members submit declarations through authorised endpoints; Maya’s dashboard shows outstanding work and exceptions.

SQS retry and recovery design: standard queues provide at-least-once delivery: a message can arrive more than once, and processing order is not guaranteed. Workers therefore need to be idempotent: receiving the same message again should not create duplicate tasks or replace a saved response.

The visibility timeout temporarily hides a received message while a worker processes it. Set it for the expected processing time and extend it for longer jobs. Delete the message only after the work has been durably recorded. Configure a dead-letter queue (DLQ) for repeated failures, and investigate the cause before redriving those messages for processing again.

For email, keep “queued”, “accepted by SES” and “delivered to the recipient’s mail server” distinct. Use an application notification key to recognise completed jobs, and retain SES delivery or bounce feedback. A timed-out send can have an uncertain outcome; reconcile it before resending, because SQS retry handling does not make an external email send exactly-once.

Tasks: break the annual-verification story into small changes

The pilot still includes the other asset-management capabilities. The tasks below decompose its annual-declaration work into smaller development tasks. Link each one to the user story, acceptance criteria and relevant TRD decision. Include tests and an expected result in each task.

Example task breakdown:

  • Provision the SQS queues and permissions. Define the work queues and their DLQs through infrastructure as code. Give each worker only the queue operations it needs. Verify that unauthorised access is denied and repeated processing failures reach the correct DLQ;
  • Create the RDS PostgreSQL migration. Add verification runs, declaration tasks and notification records. Add uniqueness constraints for each project’s annual run and each asset’s task. Verify that duplicate inserts cannot create duplicate work;
  • Implement the Java start and status endpoints. After the migration, add permission checks and run creation with an outbox event. Verify that repeated starts return the same run and denied requests leave records unchanged;
  • Configure EventBridge Scheduler. Send scheduled start commands to the dedicated SQS queue using its execution role. Implement the Java command handler to invoke the shared start service. Verify that the configured date and time zone produce the intended verification year, and that scheduled and manual starts reuse one run;
  • Build the outbox relay. Send committed events to the appropriate SQS queue using the AWS SDK for Java. Mark events as published after a successful send response. Simulate a connection failure and verify that events remain retryable without creating duplicate work;
  • Build the task-generation worker on Fargate. Receive SQS messages and save per-asset tasks with pending notification events in one transaction. Delete each message after commit. Interrupt processing before deletion and verify that redelivery still leaves one task per asset;
  • Build the SQS-to-SES notification worker. Receive notification jobs and send the task link and due date through SES. Record attempts and configure SES event publishing to update delivery status. Test a completed job being redelivered, a temporary failure and an uncertain send outcome;
  • Build the React manager screen. Connect the start button and progress view to the API. Verify that Maya can distinguish task generation from notification delivery and can see work that needs attention;
  • Implement declaration submission. Add the Java response endpoint and its permission tests. Preserve response history and verify behaviour when an asset changes holder during an open run;
  • Build the React member form. Connect the response choices to that endpoint. Verify keyboard access and that a lost or faulty report remains visible to Maya;
  • Implement reminder checks and overdue status. Use EventBridge Scheduler to enqueue periodic checks. The Java handler selects unanswered tasks and records reminder events for the notification queue. Verify that completed tasks receive no further reminders and missing responses become overdue;
  • Verify the integrated user story on AWS. Deploy the API and workers to the test ECS environment and the React build to S3 and CloudFront. Exercise the journey from start to member response and manager review. Include SQS redelivery and an SES failure, and retain the results for independent review.

Sequence work by its dependencies: the API and workers need the data model; the React screens need their API contracts. Implement reminders after tasks and responses are available. Review the complete feature as well as each small change.

Keep the connection visible: “Notify members when tasks are ready” is a PRD acceptance criterion. The queued notification flow is the TRD decision. The SQS-to-SES notification worker is a development task. Its retry test and delivery-status evidence show whether that part of the design works.

Reference toolkit · Optional

Plan evaluations for agents and AI product behaviour

Use this detail when assessing a development agent or a product capability that generates AI responses. A task is the intended job; a trial is one attempt; grading is the assessment of that attempt. Check the actual outcome and side effects as well as any score.

Evaluate AI behaviour across repeated trials

For a development agent, evaluate how it completes delivery tasks within its permitted tools and scope. For a product containing AI, evaluate the user-facing capability and its failure behaviour. Anthropic’s agent evaluation guidance distinguishes a task, repeated trials, grading and the actual outcome, and combines executable checks, model-based assessment and human judgement where each fits.

Record the dataset, model, instructions, tools and environment. Repeat representative tasks because outputs vary, and check final state and side effects, not only the response. Calibrate model-based graders against human judgement and keep regression cases for fixed failures. Agree the acceptance rule before running the evaluation, and report failures by case type; an overall pass rate can hide failures in important case types, such as unauthorised actions or invented facts.

Calibrating a model-based grader means comparing its scores with human judgements on the same cases and resolving important disagreements before relying on it. Record which users and case types the test set represents, what it misses and which failures always block acceptance. Return to independent assurance.

Reference toolkit · Optional

Provide tools, context and execution controls

Choose platform capabilities to match the tasks, data and permissions involved; a separate service for every capability is unnecessary. It gives people and agents consistent access to authorised context, reusable procedures, tools, realistic dependencies and standard commands, and keeps the evidence needed to reconstruct each action.

Platform capabilities to consider for the implementation loop
CapabilityWhat it provides and controls
Context platformCurrent organisational, architecture, domain, policy, security and technical context, with source, version, owner, freshness and access control
Skills registryTested, reusable procedures, each with a version, an owner, dependencies, evaluations and a retirement status
Tool gatewayGoverned access to tools, data and services through Model Context Protocol (MCP), a standard way to connect AI applications to tools and data, or a similar interface, with identity, allow-lists, rate limits, audit trails and data boundaries
Test containersReproducible dependencies such as databases, queues, browsers, services and models, with pinned versions and isolated data
Standard command-line and CI toolingThe same build, test, review, packaging, release and recovery commands locally and in continuous integration (CI), with structured output and meaningful exit codes
AI gatewayGoverned model access, with allow-lists, routing, authentication, model-version records, safety controls, data-residency enforcement and cost records

Design the platform around these principles:

  • Least privilege: grant access scoped to the task, and raise it only through policy-controlled routes.
  • Predictable interfaces: prefer structured inputs, machine-readable outputs, meaningful exit codes and operations that are safe to repeat.
  • Provenance throughout: keep the specifications, context versions, tools, models, prompts, code, tests, reviewers and approvals behind each outcome.
  • Safe isolation: run untrusted changes in disposable environments with synthetic or approved data.
  • Readable evidence: produce quality reports that accountable people can understand and challenge.
  • Replaceable parts: put context, skills, models, scanners and tool providers behind stable contracts.

Reference toolkit · Optional

Increase autonomy only with evidence

A mature factory is not one without people. It is one whose chosen way of working produces acceptable outcomes with the right control, evidence and recovery. Different products, and different kinds of change, can work at different levels in the same organisation.

Three ways to run the factory; each is a risk choice
ModeRole of peopleControls neededGood fit
AI as co-pilotPeople drive the work; agents suggest, generate, explain and checkNormal engineering controls, review of agent output, clear data and tool boundariesNew work, uncertain requirements, sensitive design, decisions needing high judgement
Light factoryAgents run substantial workflows; people handle exceptions and accept quality reportsStrong specifications, automated tests, specialist review, monitoring, rollback, traceabilityRepeatable delivery where risk is bounded and evidence is mature
Dark factoryPeople set goals, policy and escalation limits; routine work proceeds without themProven autonomy, formal risk classification, independent automated assurance, strict tool control, containment, auditabilityHighly standardised, unambiguous work with stable architecture, strong tests, small blast radius and proven recovery

Choose autonomy that serves the task and fits the available evidence and controls. More autonomy is not itself an improvement. Weigh safety and regulatory impact, data sensitivity, reversibility, blast radius, product ambiguity, architecture stability, test strength, monitoring, recovery time, model reliability and risk tolerance.

These modes describe possible operating arrangements, not Eitri availability or permission to bypass its human gates. Use the EDS AI Workflow for its current route and controls.

Grant autonomy per kind of action. An agent might update a low-risk dependency within a tested range, while a material schema, schedule or access-rule change still needs explicit approval. Record the delegated actions, criteria, permission limits and escalation owner before enabling automation. Agree how control failures or worsening quality suspend that delegation, and test the handback route.

Test sustained operability before expanding autonomous authority

Sustained operability means being able to keep the service running, change it and recover it over time. Before expanding autonomous release authority, run a bounded pilot that tests more than successful code generation. The team should be able to diagnose a realistic fault, make a follow-up change, restore service within agreed limits and explain the change using retained evidence. This is a recommended evidence check, not a new approval gate.

These suggested pilot checks adapt practitioner guidance; they are not evidence that greater agent autonomy improves effectiveness. Measure results and recovery under the intended conditions.

Choose pilot signals that fit the change and criticality: CI reliability (whether shared automated checks run consistently), change fail rate (the share of deployments needing immediate intervention), recovery time and whether service was actually restored, successful follow-up modifications, and completeness of the evidence trail. Compare them with feature throughput and cost per accepted change. A prototype that never reaches production does not need production-grade readiness burdens.

Note

Running without people is not the same as maturity. A dark factory without independent assurance, containment, monitoring and proven recovery is an unattended risk. Read about light and dark software factories.

Reference toolkit · Optional

Measure whether the whole loop works

No single measure shows whether delivery is improving. Speed can improve while escaped defects, policy exceptions or harm to users increase. Balance measures across flow, quality, recovery, product outcomes, system health and governance.

Suggested measures; set local measures and thresholds before relying on them
FamilyExample signalsQuestion it answers
FlowLead time, cycle time, work in progress, gate wait time, review latency, change size, deployment frequencyDoes valuable work move predictably, and where does evidence wait?
QualityFirst-pass review rate, escaped defects, mutation score, change failure rate, evaluation pass rateDoes the loop prevent and detect important failures?
RecoveryTime to detect, contain, restore and prevent recurrence; rollback success; repeat defectsCan the team limit harm and learn quickly when something fails?
ProductAdoption, task success, retention, time saved, satisfaction, error rate, harm and fairness indicatorsIs the product solving the intended user problem?
System healthAvailability, latency, cost per outcome, data quality, flaky tests, context freshness, tool failuresCan the product and factory sustain the required service?
GovernanceTraceability, policy coverage, gate bypasses, exception age, approval latency, unauthorised tool attemptsIs autonomy operating within its declared authority and risk tolerance?

Lines of code, prompts issued and tasks attempted are weak measures of productivity. Measure the flow of accepted product behaviour instead: how quickly well-defined intent becomes a safe increment, how often it is rejected or fails, whether users benefit and whether the factory improves after learning. Split measures by risk, product area, type of change and factory mode.

Use consistent delivery measures

DORA’s current delivery guidance uses five measures: change lead time, deployment frequency, failed deployment recovery time, change fail rate and deployment rework rate. Lead time runs from commit to production; recovery time concerns a failed deployment requiring intervention. Rework rate tracks unplanned deployments caused by production incidents.

Follow one application or service over time using consistent definitions. Pair delivery measures with user outcomes and operating cost. Do not rank individuals by these measures or attribute a change to AI without checking other changes in scope, staffing and process.

Worked example · Delivery measuresRead the pilot’s delivery resultsCalculate the rates and choose what to investigate next.

Maya’s application has no deployment history before launch. Establish its first baseline after launch; spreadsheet follow-up time is a separate product baseline. This fictional example compares the same service over two four-week production periods, using unchanged definitions.

Illustrative DORA comparison for the asset-management service
MeasureFirst four weeks: baselineNext four weeks: observed
Change lead timeFirst four weeks: baselineMedian commit-to-production time: 2 days.Next four weeks: observedMedian: 1 day.
Deployment frequencyFirst four weeks: baseline8 deployments ÷ 4 weeks = 2 per week.Next four weeks: observed10 ÷ 4 = 2.5 per week.
Failed deployment recovery timeFirst four weeks: baselineTwo failed deployments recovered in 30 and 60 minutes; median 45 minutes.Next four weeks: observedTwo failed deployments recovered in 20 and 40 minutes; median 30 minutes.
Change fail rateFirst four weeks: baseline2 deployments needing immediate intervention ÷ 8 = 25%.Next four weeks: observed2 ÷ 10 = 20%.
Deployment rework rateFirst four weeks: baseline2 unplanned incident-response deployments ÷ 8 = 25%.Next four weeks: observed2 ÷ 10 = 20%.

Decision: the team’s illustrative improvement target was median lead time of one day, while keeping recovery within 60 minutes and losing no saved declarations. The lead-time target was met, but two deployments still failed in each period. The lower failure percentage alone does not establish fewer incidents or a benefit from AI.

Investigate the two failures before expanding rollout. Continue checking every saved declaration remains visible to Maya; a hidden or lost report triggers containment regardless of delivery speed. Pair these figures with Maya’s follow-up effort and unresolved faulty/lost reports. Recovery medians describe the observed failures, not a guarantee for the next one; with no failed deployments, report recovery time as not observed.

These local example values are not DORA targets. Failure rate asks which deployments required intervention; rework rate asks which deployments were unplanned responses to production incidents. The same count in this example does not make the measures interchangeable.

Agree the response before the signal arrives

The following are suggested responses to investigate and adapt locally:

  • Review latency above its target or growing change size leads to checking work in progress, reviewer capacity and whether important judgement was deferred to code review. Slice work smaller, add pairing or a design review, or rebalance review capacity; do not lower independent checks merely to clear a queue.
  • Recurring defects lead to factory fixes, such as new scanner rules, better tests, updated skills or corrected context.
  • A falling mutation score prompts a review of changed tests and code before increasing autonomy, even when line coverage stays high.
  • Repeated gate bypasses lead to a governance review and can reduce autonomy automatically.
  • Worsening product outcomes prompt checks of measurement quality, adoption, task mix and operating conditions. Evidence challenging product assumptions reopens Project Discovery to review the problem, value or experience.
  • Recovery outside tolerance leads to stronger containment before deployment frequency increases.

Use the overview’s feedback signals and decisions to coordinate corrections, further investigation and changes to scope or delivery practice.

AIHow AI can help

AI can group delivery failures and operating observations from the recorded evidence. Check the original events and measurement definitions before inferring a cause, then record the next product change or workflow improvement and how its effect will be checked.

Continue with the EDS AI Workflow

For the steps, roles, skills and checks used by EDS teams, read the EDS AI Workflow (Eitri) guide.
